contents.title: Malaysia Data-Centre Approvals – June 20, 2026
contents.body:
## Approvals Recorded in June 2026

On 20 June 2026, Malaysia's Investment, Trade and Industry Ministry (MITI) published its monthly data-centre project register for May 2026. The register lists 14 approved data-centre projects with a combined committed investment of RM 9.4 billion. Of these, nine are located in Johor, three in Selangor, one in Penang and one in Negeri Sembilan. MITI states that the approvals cover a combined 412 megawatts of contracted electrical capacity.

The same register records that two previously approved projects in Johor were withdrawn by their developers in May 2026, citing grid connection timelines. MITI does not name the developers. The register states that withdrawn capacity totalled 96 megawatts.

Tenaga Nasional Berhad (TNB) published its May 2026 grid connection queue on 18 June 2026. The queue lists 31 data-centre connection applications under study, with a combined requested capacity of 2.7 gigawatts. TNB states that 11 of the 31 applications are in Johor, 9 in Selangor, 5 in Penang, 4 in Negeri Sembilan and 2 in Kedah. TNB states that the average study period for applications received in the first quarter of 2026 was 214 days.

## Grid and Water Statements

The Energy Commission (Suruhanjaya Tenaga) issued a statement on 12 June 2026 confirming that it had received 22 applications for electricity supply licences for data-centre operations between January and May 2026. The Commission states that 8 licences were issued in the period, 6 were refused and 8 remain under review. The Commission does not publish applicant names.

The National Water Services Commission (SPAN) stated on 9 June 2026 that it had received 17 applications for water supply commitments for data-centre projects in the first five months of 2026. SPAN states that 10 applications were approved, 4 were deferred pending further documentation and 3 were rejected. SPAN states that approved commitments total 38 million litres per day.

The Johor state government published a statement on 5 June 2026 stating that it had received 26 data-centre planning permission applications in the first five months of 2026 and had approved 15. The statement says the state has set a review threshold of 20 megawatts for projects requiring state-level technical review.

## Corporate Filings and Statements

TSMC filed a notification with the Malaysia Investment Development Authority (MIDA) on 3 June 2026 regarding a planned advanced packaging facility in Penang. The filing states that the facility is intended to support data-centre accelerator packaging and that construction is scheduled to begin in the first quarter of 2027. The filing does not state a capacity figure. MIDA confirmed receipt of the filing on 4 June 2026.

A joint venture registered in Singapore, identified in filings as Horizon Compute Holdings Pte Ltd, filed with the Companies Commission of Malaysia on 28 May 2026 to establish a Malaysian subsidiary. The filing lists a paid-up capital of RM 250 million and states the subsidiary's intended activity as data-centre development and operation. The filing does not name a site.

YTL Power International Berhad stated in a filing dated 11 June 2026 that its data-centre campus in Kulai, Johor, had reached 120 megawatts of operational capacity. The filing states that a further 80 megawatts is under construction and scheduled for completion in the fourth quarter of 2026.

GDS Holdings stated in a press release dated 16 June 2026 that it had signed a power purchase agreement with TNB for a 64-megawatt facility in Selangor. The release states that the agreement runs for 15 years and that commercial operation is targeted for the second quarter of 2027.

## Regional and Monetary Context

The Bank of Japan (BoJ) published its monetary policy statement on 17 June 2026, holding its policy rate unchanged. The statement does not reference Malaysia or data-centre investment. The BoJ's next scheduled policy meeting is on 30 and 31 July 2026.

Malaysia's Department of Statistics released May 2026 trade data on 19 June 2026. The data record a 14.2 per cent year-on-year increase in exports of electrical and electronic products, which the Department attributes in part to semiconductor and data-centre equipment shipments. The Department does not publish a separate data-centre equipment category.

Bank Negara Malaysia published its international reserves statement on 13 June 2026, recording reserves of USD 118.4 billion as at 31 May 2026. The statement does not reference data-centre investment.

The ASEAN Secretariat published a note on 10 June 2026 stating that member states had agreed to a common reporting template for cross-border data-centre investment statistics. The note states that the template will take effect on 1 January 2027 and that reporting will be voluntary in the first year.

## Pending Items

MITI's register states that 6 data-centre applications received in May 2026 remain under review and that decisions are expected by 31 July 2026. TNB states that it will publish its June 2026 connection queue on 18 July 2026. SPAN states that its next water commitment review is scheduled for 14 July 2026. The Johor state government states that its next planning permission decisions are scheduled for 3 July 2026. The Energy Commission states that its next licence decisions are scheduled for 24 July 2026. No further statements were recorded as of 20 June 2026.

contents.title: Analysts cut Kestrel margin estimates as the TSMC deal lands
contents.body:
Kestrel Semiconductor lost a fifth of its consensus gross margin in a single morning. On 1 October 2026, the average fiscal 2027 gross margin estimate across the five brokers covering the Singapore-based fabless designer fell to 55.2% from 58.5%, after three of the five revised their models to absorb the terms of a new wafer supply agreement with TSMC. The stock closed 4.1% lower in Taipei, its worst session since February.

The revisions were not a judgment on demand. They were arithmetic. Under the previous contract, Kestrel paid about US$19,800 for each N3P wafer. The new agreement, signed on 29 September and disclosed in a brief filing before the Taipei open, prices the same wafer at roughly US$22,500. That is a rise of 13.6%, and it lands directly on a product line that accounts for the majority of Kestrel's data-center accelerator volume.

## The prepayment is the part that worries the buy side

Analysts had expected a price increase. TSMC has been vocal about N3 and N3P capacity being effectively sold out through 2027, and Kestrel is not large enough to command the discounts available to the hyperscaler in-house design teams. What the market did not expect was the prepayment.

Kestrel agreed to advance US$1.1 billion against future wafer deliveries, payable in three instalments, the last of them due by the end of April 2027. Against Kestrel's US$2.4 billion of cash and short-term investments, that is about 46% of the balance sheet committed to a single supplier. Daniel Okafor, who covers the name for Kestrel's most cautious broker, described the structure as "a capacity option dressed as a purchase order" and cut his target price to NT$410 from NT$520.

The bull case is that the prepayment locks in allocation at a moment when N3P slots are the scarcest input in the accelerator supply chain. Kestrel's next-generation part, the K2, is scheduled to tape out in the June 2027 quarter and ramps in volume in fiscal 2028. Without secured capacity, the company would be bidding for scraps on the spot market, where lead times have stretched past forty weeks. With it, Kestrel can promise customers delivery dates, which in this market is worth more than a few points of gross margin.

## Revenue estimates went up, not down

The same morning produced a second, less-noticed revision. Analysts raised fiscal 2028 revenue estimates to US$6.4 billion from US$5.5 billion on 1 October 2026, citing the volume commitments embedded in the TSMC agreement. The contract's take-or-pay structure implies wafer purchases consistent with roughly 40% more accelerator shipments than the previous model assumed.

That combination, higher revenue and lower margin, is the classic signature of a company trading profitability for scale. Mei-Ling Tan of the Taipei desk at a regional brokerage raised her fiscal 2028 revenue number by 16% while cutting her gross margin assumption by 310 basis points. "The mix is shifting toward a larger, lower-margin customer set," she wrote. "We would rather own the volume than the margin, but we are not going to pretend the margin is intact."

Two of the five analysts kept their margin estimates unchanged, arguing that the price increase will be offset by a richer product mix in the second half of fiscal 2027, when the higher-margin K2 variant enters production. Both, however, flagged the prepayment as a risk factor in their notes. The consensus, for now, sits with the majority.

## What the Bank of Japan has to do with it

The timing of the disclosure has a macro dimension that Kestrel's investors did not ask for. The yen's slide past 165 against the dollar has made TSMC's Japanese advanced packaging subsidiary, AP1, more cost-competitive in dollar terms, and the Bank of Japan's reluctance to tighten further has kept the currency weak. TSMC has used that cost advantage to hold the line on packaging prices even as wafer prices rise. For Kestrel, that is a small mercy: the packaging step on the K2 is quoted in yen, and the currency move offsets perhaps 80 basis points of the wafer increase.

But the BoJ is the wild card. If the central bank signals a faster normalization path at its December meeting, the yen strengthens, AP1's dollar costs rise, and TSMC has historically passed such moves through to fabless customers at the next contract reset. Kestrel's agreement runs through fiscal 2029, but it contains a currency-adjustment clause that two of the analysts flagged as under-modeled.

## The cash question

Kestrel ended the September quarter with US$2.4 billion in cash and short-term investments and no debt. The US$1.1 billion prepayment is affordable. It is not free. The company had earmarked roughly US$700 million of that cash for a share repurchase program announced in July, and the buyback is now expected to be halved or suspended. Okafor estimates the forgone repurchase adds about 1.5% to fiscal 2028 earnings per share dilution, a figure he called "annoying but not thesis-changing."

The more consequential question is what happens if the K2 slips. The prepayment is not refundable, and the take-or-pay volumes begin in the December 2027 quarter. If Kestrel's own customers push out their orders, the company eats the wafers or pays for them anyway. That scenario is not in any published model, but it is the reason the stock's implied volatility on twelve-month options jumped to 48% from 36% on the day of the filing.

For now, the sell side has done what the sell side does: marked the margin down, marked the revenue up, and moved on. The next data point is Kestrel's fiscal fourth-quarter earnings call on 12 November, when management is expected to give its first formal guidance for fiscal 2027. Until then, the 55.2% consensus is a placeholder, and everyone knows it.

The previous contract covered 16,000 wafers a month. On July 25, 2026, Kestrel Semiconductor published its quarterly exchange filings with the Taiwan Stock Exchange and the Tokyo Stock Exchange. The filings, dated July 24, 2026, cover the period from April 1 to June 30, 2026. Kestrel reported net revenue of NT$142.3 billion for the quarter, a figure that appears in the consolidated income statement on page 12 of the Taiwan filing. The company also disclosed a gross margin of 48.7 percent, down from 51.2 percent in the same quarter of 2025. Operating income was NT$38.9 billion, and net income was NT$31.4 billion. These figures are stated in the filing without adjustment for foreign exchange fluctuations. A Kestrel statement dated 2 September 2026 says Phase 2 reached its rated capacity on 28 August 2026. The statement gives no unit figures. A second statement dated 20 September 2026 says the plant operated at 92 per cent of rated capacity in the week ending 18 September 2026. The record states no customer lead times. The practice is not new. Foundries and their largest customers have used advance payments for decades, particularly when a customer needs assurance that a new process node will be available in volume. The prepayment can cover a portion of the total contract value or the entire amount. It can be refundable or non-refundable, depending on the terms. Public disclosures rarely include the full contract, so the exact terms are often known only to the parties and their auditors. I spent most of the week before the September meeting staring at the same question every rates strategist was asking: how much of this was already in the curve? My honest answer, as of the close on 17 September 2026, was most of it. The hike was roughly 85% priced by 17 September 2026, so the 9 bp rise in the 10-year yield on 18 September 2026 reflects guidance, not the move itself. That distinction matters more than the headline number, and it is the thing I want to unpack here. Take a hall with an IT load of 4.2 MW. Suppose the operators run a conventional chilled-water plant with a design PUE of 1.45. That gives a total facility load of 6.09 MW, of which 1.89 MW is cooling and losses. Now suppose they decide to economise by admitting outside air at 32 degrees Celsius and 80 percent relative humidity, which is a typical afternoon in Kuala Lumpur or Jakarta. This round allocated a little over 600 MW of new capacity across roughly two dozen buyers. Most contracts run for 21 years, which matches the economic life the developers assume for their panels. The buyers are a predictable mix: data-centre operators in Johor, two glove makers, a brewery, several electronics plants in Kulim and Perak, and one cement works that I suspect signed mainly for the press coverage. Speaking as an ex-central banker, I've learned to be wary of over-reading any single policy meeting. The Bank of Japan's gathering on 2026-09-30 was no exception. The statement itself was, in many ways, a masterclass in continuity. Yet the market's reaction was anything but continuous. In this newsletter, I will try to separate what the Bank actually said from what the market heard, and I will flag where my own interpretation remains uncertain.
